headline: Ant: A new JavaScript runtime with Node-compatible API, 9MB binary, and Wasm support
summary: Ant is a lightweight JavaScript runtime built from scratch, offering a Node-compatible API, VM-isolated sandbox, and built-in Wasm support. It runs npm packages and TypeScript from a single 9MB binary.
details: Ant is a new JavaScript runtime designed for efficiency, packaged as a single 9MB binary. It allows developers to run real npm packages and TypeScript directly, offering a streamlined development experience.

Built from scratch on its own engine, Ant provides a Node-compatible API, ensuring familiarity for existing JavaScript developers. It also features a VM-isolated sandbox for enhanced security and built-in WebAssembly (Wasm) support.
caption:
Run npm packages and TypeScript from a single 9MB binary. Meet Ant, a new JavaScript runtime built from scratch.

Ant is a new JavaScript runtime designed for efficiency, packaged as a single 9MB binary. It allows developers to run real npm packages and TypeScript directly, offering a streamlined development experience.

Built from scratch on its own engine, Ant provides a Node-compatible API, ensuring familiarity for existing JavaScript developers. It also features a VM-isolated sandbox for enhanced security and built-in WebAssembly (Wasm) support.

headline_marked: [[This 3D-printed electric motorbike folds into your luggage]] — creator warns it is 'super fast'
headline: This 3D-printed electric motorbike folds into your luggage — creator warns it is 'super fast'
summary: Ivan Miranda has released design files for his re-engineered Mirandetta, a 3D-printed electric motorbike that breaks down to fit inside a suitcase. The creator cautions it's "way too fast" for its size.
details: Ivan Miranda has released the design files for the Mirandetta, a 3D-printed electric motorbike. This re-engineered vehicle is designed to break down and fit inside a standard suitcase, making it a unique travel solution. The design files are available for $40 through his website, ivanmiranda.com.

The original Mirandetta was built in about 10 days as a "travel hack" to be the smallest adult-ridable motorbike that could fit into checked luggage. The new design standardizes parts for easier replication by makers, replacing original aluminum axles and a metal steering column with 3D-printed components.

Miranda also standardized lighting using off-the-shelf T10 automotive sockets and bulbs, reducing the number of distinct screws needed. Crucially, every part is constrained to print on a single 300mm x 300mm build volume, making it accessible for many 3D printers like the Prusa CORE One L.

The wheels utilize lawnmower tires, which are typically flat-profiled. Miranda printed the rims narrower than standard, allowing the tire's sidewalls to round into a usable profile for cornering once inflated, despite the unusual tire choice.

Braking is handled by floating motorcycle discs, which can be modified to accommodate a wider center bore for the printed axle. A belt drive powers the rear wheel, and a 10K linear potentiometer acts as the throttle, controlled via an Arduino to the motor's electronic speed controller.

Power comes from two hot-swappable 36V cordless tool battery packs, simplifying airport security checks. A DC-DC converter steps down the voltage to 12V for the horn and lights. Without batteries, the finished bike weighs just over 14kg.

While the bike disassembles for travel, it cannot be folded while assembled. Miranda won a suitcase-build contest at Prague Maker Faire with the original machine. He sells the files as-is, emphasizing it's a "complicated hobby build" not intended as a production design.
